uncited: Sparse and Efficient Representations address the computational and memory bottlenecks of dense, monolithic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by decomposing the scene representation into smaller, localized, or structured components.
This family enables scalable training for large-scale scenes and faster inference through spatial partitioning, explicit sparse grids, or generalized 2D projections.

All methods in this family share the mechanism of mapping 6D input coordinates (3D position $\mathbf{x}$ and 2D viewing direction $\mathbf{d}$) to 4D output values (density $\sigma$ and color $\mathbf{c}$) using a differentiable neural network.
This allows the radiance field to be optimized through the volumetric rendering integral.
Raw coordinates $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{d}$ are rarely used directly due to the spectral bias of MLPs, which struggle to fit high-frequency details.
**Density Network:** Takes the encoded position $\gamma(\mathbf{x})$ as input.

**Color Network:** Takes the encoded position $\gamma(\mathbf{x})$, the raw viewing direction $\mathbf{d}$, and the intermediate feature vector from the density network (usually the output of the last hidden layer before the density head) as input.
During training, rays are sampled at points $\mathbf{x}_i$ along the ray.
Color MLP is shared across all GPUs using Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) to ensure consistent color prediction for novel views.
Appearance Embedding is shared across GPUs; set to zero during novel-view rendering if enabled during training.

The concept of decomposing NeRF representations for efficiency originated with KiloNeRF, which demonstrated that replacing a single large MLP with thousands of small MLPs could accelerate rendering by three orders of magnitude without sacrificing visual quality [S2].
